entry.title: Keep the Feedback You Disagreed With
entry.summary: There is feedback you were given once that you decided was wrong. Do not throw it away. It happens to everyone. Someone tells you that you are too blunt in reviews, or too slow to commit to a decision, or that you go too deep into detail in meetings. You think about it honestly and you conclude they have misread you. Maybe they had. Maybe they were measuring you against themselves, or they caught you on your worst week, or they were repeating something they heard secondhand. So you set it aside, which is allowed. You do not have to act on everything you are told. But do not delete it. Write it down, put a date next to it, and come back to it in six months. Here is why. Some feedback is wrong. Some feedback is early. In the moment those two feel identical, because both arrive as something that does not match how you see yourself. The early kind is the valuable kind. Somebody noticed a pattern before you had enough examples of it to believe them. Six months later you have the examples. You read the note again and it lands completely differently, because now you have three incidents to hold it against instead of none. I have watched people have that moment and it is always the same. A quiet, slightly annoyed, oh. They were right. I just could not see it yet. The ones that really were wrong turn out to be useful too. After two or three readings you can say, with evidence rather than defensiveness, that you have checked this one more than once and it does not hold. That is a far stronger place to stand than a flat denial in the moment. And watch for repeats. A note you dismissed from one person is easy to write off. The same note from three unrelated people across two years is not an opinion about you. It is a measurement. Keep the file. Be honest when you read it. The feedback you argued with is usually the feedback most worth revisiting. – Asael Shinder

entry.title: Be Confident in How You Work, Not What You Know
entry.summary: Ground your confidence in how you work, not in what you currently know. Knowledge based confidence is a trap, and it gets more dangerous the better you get. You learn a stack deeply, you become the person everyone asks, and your sense of being competent quietly fuses with that specific body of facts. Then the company changes direction, or the tool is replaced, or you move teams, and your confidence walks out of the door with the thing you knew. You have seen this happen to people with fifteen years behind them. They are not less capable than they were. They simply tied their sense of themselves to a body of knowledge that had an expiry date, and nobody warned them it did. The durable version sounds different. It sounds like this. I do not know this yet, and I know how I find out. That sentence rests on evidence you can actually collect. You have learned hard things before. You have opened unfamiliar code and made sense of it. You have walked into a domain you knew nothing about and been useful inside a month. You have been the lost new person several times, and you came out the other side every time. So keep track of that. Not a list of technologies. A list of the times you were lost and then were not. How long it took. What you did first. Who you asked. When the next unfamiliar thing arrives, you are not guessing whether you can handle it. You have a record. This changes what you say yes to. If your confidence lives in what you know, every new area is a threat to your identity, so you defend your corner and call it focus. If it lives in how you work, unfamiliar work is just the ordinary beginning of something, mildly uncomfortable and entirely survivable. It also makes you easier to be around. People who need to be the expert in the room are exhausting. People who can say I have no idea, let me go and find out, are the ones everybody wants on the hard projects. What you know will keep turning over. How you work is yours to keep. – Asael Shinder

entry.summary: The history of this F3SPR extractor dates back to 2014, when it started as a small feature within a larger data parsing tool to handle specific scene data. Between 2017 and 2019, it evolved into a standalone dedicated extractor. entry.title: Solana v1 Transactions Explained: Size Limits and Breaking Changes
entry.summary: Transaction v1 raises Solana's maximum transaction size from 1,232 bytes to 4,096 bytes and removes Address Lookup Tables. Here is what changes for applications that read Solana data, and what changes for applications that send it.
